title: How Computers Solve Problems
description: Write down a procedure precisely enough that something without judgement could follow it, then work out how long it would take.
audience: Someone who uses computers daily and wants to understand how a program decides what to do, without learning a language first.

modules.title: Writing a procedure
modules.summary: Turning something you know how to do into steps something else could follow.

concepts.title: Algorithm
concepts.summary: A finite sequence of unambiguous steps that ends with an answer.

concepts.title: Sequence
concepts.summary: Steps happen in order, and the order changes the result.

concepts.title: Conditional branch
concepts.summary: A step that chooses between two paths based on a test.

concepts.title: Loop
concepts.summary: A step repeated until a condition stops it.

lessons.title: Steps a machine could follow
lessons.outcome: Spot the ambiguity in an everyday instruction and rewrite it so it cannot be misread.
outline: Hook: follow 'make toast' literally and see where it fails
Explain what makes a step unambiguous
Definition: algorithm
Worked example: rewriting one vague step
Interact: order the steps of a familiar task
Check: pick the instruction that is still ambiguous
Close: precision is the whole job

lessons.title: Choosing between paths
lessons.outcome: Trace a procedure containing a test, and predict which branch runs for given inputs.
outline: Hook: predict what a two-branch rule does with an edge-case input
Explain the test and its two outcomes
Worked example: tracing a flow diagram by hand
Interact: tap the branch taken for a given input
Check: the input that takes the unexpected path
Close: the edge cases are where branches go wrong

lessons.title: Doing it again
lessons.outcome: Say what makes a loop stop, and identify the change that would make it never stop.
outline: Hook: what would make this loop run forever?
Explain the loop condition and the thing that changes
Worked example: counting down, traced step by step
Interact: order the steps of one pass through a loop
Check: the edit that removes the exit
Close: every loop needs something that moves toward stopping

modules.title: How long it takes
modules.summary: Why two procedures that both work are not equally good.

concepts.title: Linear search
concepts.summary: Checking every item in turn until the target is found.

concepts.title: Binary search
concepts.summary: Halving a sorted range repeatedly, which is why order is worth paying for.

concepts.title: Growth
concepts.summary: How the work rises as the input gets bigger, which is what actually matters.

lessons.title: Looking things up
lessons.outcome: Count the checks a linear search makes in the best and worst cases.
outline: Hook: how many names might you read to find one in an unsorted list of 100?
Explain the best, worst and typical case
Worked example: counting checks on a short list
Interact: plot the worst-case checks against list length
Check: the worst case for a list of 50
Close: worst case is the promise you can make

lessons.title: Halving the problem
lessons.outcome: Explain why binary search needs a sorted list and how few checks it takes.
outline: Hook: guess a number between 1 and 100 in seven questions
Explain halving and why sorting is the price
Worked example: seven halvings of 100
Interact: order the steps of one binary search
Check: how many checks for a list of 1000
Close: an assumption bought a large speed-up

lessons.title: When the input grows
lessons.outcome: Compare how two procedures behave as the input gets large, rather than at one size.
outline: Hook: one method wins on ten items and loses on ten thousand
Explain growth as the shape of the curve
Worked example: the two curves side by side
Interact: place the point where the slower method overtakes
Check: which method to choose for a large input
Close: choose for the size you will actually have
